highlights: Emperor Hirohito opened the 90th Imperial Diet speaking colloquial Japanese for the first time and submitted the government's draft revised constitution, while Prime Minister Yoshida outlined government policies.
Eight newly elected House of Representatives members were disqualified under the Purge Directive, and several peers were also purged; the Demobilization Board was created.
At the IMTFE, Chief Prosecutor Joseph B. Keenan delivered the opening statement, and defendant Yosuke Matsuoka died; SCAP also ordered 56 war crime suspects arrested.
Urban food deficits forced SCAP to release 47,807 long tons of imported cereals and flour, while staple food reserves fell to 45.3 days.
The first postwar American raw cotton arrived (21,712 bales), lifting cotton weaving 50 percent for export, though coal shortages continued to restrict heavy industry.
SCAP ordered the monopolistic Japan Lumber Company dissolved; May coal output of 1,695,000 metric tons fell below minimum quotas.
Registered union membership reached 2,695,988 in 7,207 unions, the April census counted 5,600,000 unemployed, and the Cabinet approved the Labor Disputes Adjustment Bill.
Strict quarantine contained cholera outbreaks on Tsushima and in Kyushu, 16,000,000 people were revaccinated against smallpox, and cumulative repatriates reached 3,685,378.

sections.summary: Title pages, table of contents, and list of charts, maps and graphs for Summation No. 9 (June 1946).
sections.title: Front matter

sections.summary: June 1946 overview: the 90th Diet opened with the draft constitution, eight members were purged, raw cotton arrived, food reserves fell to 45.3 days, and cholera was quarantined in Kyushu.
sections.title: Part I: General

sections.summary: SCAP reported no changes in its non-military organization during June 1946.
sections.title: Organization Under SCAP

sections.summary: The 90th Imperial Diet opened with the Emperor speaking in colloquial Japanese and receiving the draft constitution. SCAP conferred with 31 women Diet members, eight members were purged, and the Demobilization Board was created.
sections.title: Political Activities

sections.summary: Fishing grounds were extended, while coal and lumber output stayed below target. First American raw cotton arrived, staple food reserves fell to 45.3 days, and currency circulation reached ¥40,644,000,000.
sections.title: Economic Activities

sections.summary: Public relief assisted 2,182,662 people and cumulative repatriates reached 3,685,378. Teacher screening began in Chiba, the new Teachers' Manual was published, and Kyushu cholera outbreaks were quarantined.
sections.title: Social Activities

sections.summary: Political part: the 90th Diet and draft constitution, purge of eight members, Ueno black-market raid, 1,550 occupation court cases, and Keenan's IMTFE opening statement with Matsuoka's death.
sections.title: Part II: Political

sections.summary: The 90th Diet convened as the Emperor submitted the draft constitution and Prime Minister Yoshida outlined policy. Eight Diet members and several peers were purged; the Demobilization Board was established; the Emperor toured Chiba and Shizuoka.
sections.title: Government and Civil Administration

sections.summary: Mass demonstrations subsided after SCAP warnings, police raided Tokyo's Ueno black market, and lethal bootleg liquor was targeted. Police decentralization recommendations were submitted; prison death rates stayed critically high.
sections.title: Public Safety and Intelligence

sections.summary: Occupation courts heard 1,550 cases and SCAP ordered 56 war crime suspects arrested. At the IMTFE, Chief Prosecutor Keenan gave opening statements, witnesses testified on militarism, and defendant Yosuke Matsuoka died.
sections.title: Legal and War Crimes

sections.summary: Economic part: Japan Lumber Company dissolved, May coal at 1,695,000 tons, first raw cotton, 47,807 long tons of emergency cereals, 2,695,988 union members, and 10 zaibatsu families' property impounded.
sections.title: Part III: Economic

sections.summary: A reconnaissance soil survey of Kyushu was completed and SCAP doubled authorized offshore fishing and whaling areas. Hokkaido herring catches reached 207,947 metric tons; ko-ayu fry were transplanted from Lake Biwa.
sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries

sections.summary: SCAP ordered the monopolistic Japan Lumber Company dissolved. May coal output of 1,695,000 metric tons missed minimum quotas for lack of food, and a petroleum committee estimated reserves at 10,000,000 kiloliters.
sections.title: Forestry and Mining

sections.summary: Pig iron, steel, aluminum and cement output rose, but coal shortages restricted refining and chemicals. Nitrogenous fertilizer reached half of prewar peak and 250 merchant vessels were repaired.
sections.title: Heavy Industries

sections.summary: Canned fish and flour milling rose despite fuel and container shortages. Paper, sheet glass and bicycle output increased, and 1,272 truck chassis plus growing farm implement supplies were manufactured.
sections.title: Manufacturing

sections.summary: First postwar American raw cotton arrived, raising cotton weaving 50 percent for export. Raw silk reached 7,540 bales, rayon pulp manufacture resumed, and silk fabric output more than doubled.
sections.title: Textile Industries

sections.summary: Rail freight rose to 8,527,200 metric tons and coastal shipping dipped slightly. Hydroelectric power was ample, but 70 percent of municipal gas capacity sat idle for lack of coal.
sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities

sections.summary: An Imperial ordinance raised the Board of Communications to a Ministry from 1 July. Postal and telephone rates rose, radio receiver output jumped 40 percent, and the 400,000-member All Japan Communications Workers' Union was inaugurated.
sections.title: Communications

sections.summary: The Cabinet approved the Labor Disputes Adjustment Bill; union membership reached 2,695,988 in 7,207 unions. The April census found 5,600,000 totally or partially unemployed, and a separate Ministry of Labor was planned.
sections.title: Labor

sections.summary: Arrival of 21,712 bales of American raw cotton began the textile export-import program. June exports included 11,053 bales of raw silk and 70,000 tons of coal; imports included 60,000 tons of food grains.
sections.title: Imports and Exports

sections.summary: Urban food deficits forced SCAP to release 47,807 long tons of imported cereals and flour. New vegetable ceilings ended subsidies, rubber goods prices rose, and economic police logged 144,353 rationing and price violations.
sections.title: Rationing and Price Control

sections.summary: Bank of Japan note issue reached ¥40,644,000,000 as daily growth slowed. The government ran on temporary budgets and short-term loans, local tax reform aimed at ¥3,327,000,000, and national debt hit ¥203,064,000,000.
sections.title: Finance

sections.summary: SCAP impounded properties of 10 zaibatsu families, put four second-line holding companies under surveillance, and added 17 holding companies to the restricted schedule. Custody covered 594 potential reparations facilities and ¥63,024,347 in war criminal assets.
sections.title: Property Control and Reparations

sections.summary: Social part: welfare relief and repatriation (3,685,378 returned), cholera quarantine in Tsushima and Kyushu, smallpox revaccination of 16,000,000, Chiba teacher screening and the new Teachers' Manual.
sections.title: Part IV: Social

sections.summary: Relief assisted 2,182,493 people and repatriates totaled 3,685,378. Port quarantines and sanitary cordons contained cholera in Tsushima and Kyushu, 16,000,000 were revaccinated against smallpox, and DDT duster production expanded.
sections.title: Public Health and Welfare

sections.summary: Teacher screening began in Chiba Prefecture, the Ministry of Education issued the new democratic Teachers' Manual, and Imperial portrait depositories were removed from schools. Tokyo trials and constitution debates dominated the media.
sections.title: Education, Religion and Media of Expression

summary: Summation No. 9 covers non-military activities across occupied Japan during June 1946, highlighting political democratization, acute economic distress, and critical public health interventions. Politically, the 90th Imperial Diet opened under the new Yoshida Cabinet, with Emperor Hirohito delivering an unprecedented opening address in colloquial Japanese and formally submitting the draft revised constitution. SCAP and the Japanese government intensified the political purge, disqualifying prominent Diet members, while the International Military Tribunal for the Far East commenced its substantive prosecution phase. Economically, Japan faced a severe food crisis characterized by depleted urban rice stocks and widespread absenteeism, prompting emergency SCAP releases of 47,807 long tons of imported food. Industrial recovery was inaugurated by the arrival of the first postwar shipments of American raw cotton, even as critical shortages of coal and raw materials hindered heavy manufacturing. Meanwhile, union membership expanded to 2.7 million workers, and major holding company properties were impounded. Socially, authorities contained cholera outbreaks in Kyushu through strict maritime quarantine and launched nationwide teacher screening. For historians, the report provides invaluable data on constitutional deliberations, labor unrest, zaibatsu dissolution, and food relief logistics.
